SECTION 6.1

Possible values.
Weighted averages.

A random variable is a numerical measure of an experiment’s outcome. Its value is determined by chance.

Discrete

A finite or countable number of possible values.

Examples: bulbs that burn out among 10 bulbs; leaves on a selected oak tree.

Continuous

Values along an uninterrupted interval.

Example: time between calls to 911.

Is it a probability distribution?

Every probability must be between 0 and 1 inclusive, and the probabilities must sum to 1.

MOVIE-COUNT EXAMPLE

The mean and variability

x = 0, 1, …, 5

The notes give this distribution for monthly movie counts. Select a bar to inspect its contribution to the mean.

Select a bar above to see xP(x).
μX = E(X) = Σ xP(x)
σX² = Σ (x − μX)²P(x)
σX = √[Σ (x − μX)²P(x)]

Build the mean and standard deviation

First calculate xP(x) and sum that column to find μX = 1.49. Then subtract the mean from each x, square each deviation, and weight it by P(x). Enter up to six decimal places in the table.

The mean is a long-run average and need not be a possible individual count. The most likely count is 1.

Expected net gain: insurance

A one-year policy has a $530 premium and a $250,000 benefit. The survival probability in the notes is 0.99791.

OutcomeCompany’s net gainProbability
Survives$5300.99791
Does not survive−$249,4700.00209
Calculate and interpret E(X)

E(X) = 530(0.99791) − 249,470(0.00209) = $7.50 per policy.

This is the average net gain over many similar policies under this model. One individual policy produces either $530 or −$249,470.

Now switch perspectives: What is the expected net monetary gain to the policyholder/beneficiary? Try the new final question in Workshop 15.

SECTION 6.1 · MEAN OF A DISCRETE RANDOM VARIABLE

Watch the average
find its balance.

Repeat an experiment independently and record the value of X each time.

From individual outcomes to a long-run mean

Suppose an experiment is repeated n independent times and the value of the random variable X is recorded. As the number of repetitions increases, the mean value of the trials approaches μX, the mean of X.

Let x1 be the value after the first experiment, x2 after the second experiment, and so on.

x̄n = (x1 + x2 + ⋯ + xn) / n

The difference between x̄n and μX tends toward 0 as n increases. The difference can fluctuate along the way; it does not have to decrease after every trial.

Outcomes included in the event Other outcomes

P(X = x) = C(n,x)px(1 − p)n−x
C(n,x) = n! / [x!(n − x)!]
See the probability table

Use R in Posit Cloud

Open Posit Cloud ↗

Open your RStudio project and enter a command in the Console. dbinom finds an exact binomial probability; pbinom adds probabilities up to and including a count. No additional packages are needed.

EventR command
Exactly k: P(X = k)dbinom(k, size = n, prob = p)
Fewer than k: P(X < k)pbinom(k - 1, size = n, prob = p)
At most k: P(X ≤ k)pbinom(k, size = n, prob = p)
At least k: P(X ≥ k)pbinom(k - 1, size = n, prob = p, lower.tail = FALSE)
More than k: P(X > k)pbinom(k, size = n, prob = p, lower.tail = FALSE)

Replace n, p, and k with the problem’s values. The lab above creates the command for your selected event.

Why do we multiply by C(n,x)?

For four flights, one sequence with three on-time flights is S, S, F, S. Its probability is 0.79³ × 0.21. There are four sequences with three successes.

F S S SS F S SS S F SS S S F
Combine all four paths

P(X = 3) = 4(0.79³)(0.21) = 0.4142. P(X = 4) = 0.79⁴ = 0.3895.

Mean, variation, and unusual results

μX = np   ·   σX = √[np(1 − p)]

The notes use np(1 − p) > 10 as a rule of thumb for an approximately bell-shaped distribution. For a bell-shaped distribution, about 95% of values lie within μX ± 2σX.

For 400 households and p = 0.35: μ = 140, σ ≈ 9.54, and the approximate limits are 120.92 to 159.08. An observed count of 162 is unusually high by this approximate rule.
